**Source:** https://www.scienceforsport.com/carbohydrate-loading-for-endurance-still-a-good-practice/
**Title:** Carbohydrate loading for endurance - still a good practice?

# Carbohydrate loading for endurance – still a good practice?

Having a basic understanding of how carbohydrates are used during exercise can take your training and performance to the next level, and carb loading is a piece of the puzzle

## Carbohydrates – to load or not to load?

Back in high school, my water polo team hosted spaghetti nights, where the team would load up on carbohydrates the night before a big game. Maybe you’ve had spaghetti nights of your own, or perhaps heard of carbohydrate loading somewhere along the way, but is it still the best practice?

Having a basic understanding of how carbohydrates are used during exercise can take your training and performance to the next level, and carb loading is a piece of the puzzle. Let’s start by defining carbohydrates, then discuss how the body uses carbohydrates during exercise and explore what the research says about carb loading for performance.

## Types of Carbohydrates

Carbohydrates are found in grains (e.g., oatmeal, farro, barley, quinoa), fruit (e.g., whole fruits and fruit juice), milk, beans, starchy vegetables (e.g., potatoes, peas, and corn), sweets (e.g., cakes, cookies, candy), and sugary beverages.

There are two main types of carbohydrates when we think practically: simple and complex. Simple carbohydrates are foods lacking fibre, such as fruit juice and sweets. Complex carbohydrates contain fibre, such as oatmeal and whole fruit. Carbohydrates are rated on a scale called the glycemic index (GI), which represents how quickly a carbohydrate-containing food increases blood sugar levels after ingestion. Low glycemic foods include green vegetables, most fruits, beans and whole grains. High glycemic foods include white rice, white breads, and white potatoes. For health benefits, such as reducing the risk of Type 2 Diabetes, our diets should contain mostly complex/low GI carbohydrates. However, in some cases, such as playing sports or exercising, choosing simple carbohydrates/high GI foods is more optimal. We will discuss that in the next section.

## What’s the science on carb loading (aka – eating that plate of pasta)?

The concept of carb loading aims to increase the stored muscle glycogen in an effort to prolong endurance and/or improve performance. Low glycogen training has been shown to negatively impact exercise intensity in both anaerobic (doesn’t need oxygen to produce energy, e.g. resistance training) and aerobic (needs oxygen to produce energy, e.g. endurance training) exercise. Maximising glycogen stores can reduce fatigue during both anaerobic and aerobic exercise. However, most of the promising research shows results in aerobic, endurance-based activities.

*Carb loading for short-duration activity*

Very few studies have investigated the impact of carb loading on short-duration anaerobic performance. A study in male basketball players found no difference in peak power after seven days of carb loading following a four-week low carbohydrate diet. While carbohydrate loading didn’t produce higher peak power, the results from the study have implications for the importance of adequate glucose availability. After following the four-week low carbohydrate diet, the players’ performance decreased. However, after seven days of carbohydrate loading and replenishing glycogen storage, peak power returned to baseline. This means carbohydrate loading following a four-week low carb diet is effective at recovering baseline anaerobic power, emphasising the importance of glucose availability for optimal performance. Another research study looked at the impact of carb loading on jump squat power and found no improvement. So, we can conclude carb loading is not necessary for anaerobic, short-duration exercise but the amount of glucose available at the start of an activity is an important factor.

*Carb loading for long-duration activity*

The effects of carbohydrate loading on long-duration endurance exercise have garnered much more attention in the research world. However, the results differ depending on the event distance/duration and population studied. It’s been found that after an 80-minute rugby game, glycogen stores are no different in players who carb-load for 36-hours before the game to players who don’t. In other research based on individual running race times, carbohydrate loading failed to improve times for 10km and 25km treadmill runs. However, carbohydrate loading prior to a 30km cross-country run and a 30km treadmill run limited fatigue in well-trained athletes. Therefore, carbohydrate loading extends the time to glycogen depletion in running events longer than 30 km, ultimately allowing athletes to maintain race speed for a longer duration and improve race times. It appears endurance activities greater than 90 minutes support the practice of carbohydrate loading as an effective strategy to improve performance and exercise capacity.

*Gender differences*

There appears to be some discrepancies between women and men using glycogen stores during activity. Women tend to have lower resting muscle glycogen concentrations, which can impact the benefits of carbohydrate loading. Research has shown large differences in these benefits when comparing males and females. When both sexes followed a high carbohydrate diet (~75% of calories from carbohydrate foods), cycling performance increased by 45% in males and only 5% in females. Further, males managed to increase their glycogen stores by 41%, while there were no changes among females.

Knowing this, it may be beneficial for women to increase total calorie and carbohydrate ingestion during the loading phase to maximise glycogen stores.

## Other considerations

An important factor to consider for carbohydrate utilisation during endurance exercise is the glycogen availability beforehand. Skeletal muscle has the ability to increase the amount of glycogen stores through training and diet. However, this does not happen overnight and needs 24-48 hours of high carbohydrate intake to occur.

While carb loading tends to favour performance benefits for endurance events greater than 90 minutes, it is just one dietary manipulation method in the tool kit for athletes. Athletes should plan their carbohydrate intake based on sport-specific and goal-specific outcomes. Overall carbohydrate intake is important pre-, post-, and possibly during (events lasting longer than 60 minutes) physical activity.

Another benefit of adequate glycogen availability for endurance exercise is improved skeletal muscle repair and recovery. Higher glycogen stores improve post-exercise muscle recovery. So, not only will that extra serving of spaghetti help you tick off that bucket list item of running a marathon, but it will aid in your recovery afterward, too – and you’ll need all the help you can get!

## Summing up the pros and cons of carbs

The current research doesn’t have a clear answer, but promising results appear to benefit endurance exercise greater than 30km distances. Different results are likely contributed to small sample sizes, sport-specification, and population (e.g. highly trained athletes/males). Further, protocols for carbohydrate loading differ in research and practice. In most practices from our sport teams growing up, carb loading took place one night before the event, whereas research protocols vary, with seven days of carb loading and tapering training sessions (gradually reducing the amount of training) for 24-48 hours leading up to the event. Maybe we should have a week of spaghetti nights instead of one night before to increase glycogen concentrations more effectively! More seriously, conclusions drawn from the research imply carb loading is only one piece of the dietary puzzle that can advance performance for endurance athletes.

So, what are the practical applications for increasing glycogen storage?

The recommended dose for higher carbohydrate intake is 8-12 grams per kilogram of body weight. For example, an athlete who weighs 85kg should consume around 680-850 grams of carbohydrates. Consuming high GI foods appears to promote an increase in glycogen stores in athletes. The most important factor for carbohydrate loading is meeting the overall daily individual carbohydrate needs.

Carb loading timing strategies to increase the amount of glycogen stores include:

- Exercise resulting in exhaustion followed by several days of high carbohydrate intake
- An exercise taper combined with several days of increased carbohydrate intake
- A 24-48-hour high carbohydrate intake for trained athletes

While carb loading can be an effective strategy to improve your endurance performance, a holistic approach to carbohydrate availability is most important.

*Key takeaways*

*and*carbohydrate intake during the loading phase

**Source:** https://www.precisionhydration.com/performance-advice/nutrition/the-art-of-carb-loading-for-endurance-athletes/
**Title:** The art of carb loading for endurance athletes

# The art of carb loading for endurance athletes

Pro athlete Dougal Allan shares his experiences of trial and error to nail the perfect pre-race carb load...

Carb loading has to be one of the best things about being an athlete, right? When else in life are you advised to go and eat plenty of rice and pasta, all in the name of performance? In an added bonus, your carb load coincides with a time when the coach is instructing you to do less training and exercise.

Do less exercise, eat plenty of food — what's not to like about that? In reality, there's an art to nailing an eating strategy that leaves you feeling confident leading into a big event.

### What is carb loading?

Carb loading refers to spending the last few days before a key event focusing our food intake on more carbohydrate-rich foods (such as potatoes, pasta, rice, and bread) in an effort to ‘super-compensate’ our glycogen stores. Glycogen is the form in which carbohydrates are stored within the liver and muscles, ready to fuel our race-day efforts.

During the final few days leading up to an event like an IRONMAN® or the Coast to Coast World Multisport Champs, my favourite dishes included:

- Oats or peanut butter and banana on toast for breakfast
- Rice, potato or pasta-based lunches and dinners, typically featuring white meat like chicken or fish and some vegetables
- To further boost my carbohydrate intake, I snacked on items like bananas, muesli bars, cereal, and toast with honey or jam throughout the day
- I also sipped on sports drinks to help top up my carbohydrate levels and ensure my electrolyte requirements were met

### Quality over quantity

These dishes made sense given they were carbohydrate-rich and also lower in fat and fibre. It took me a few years to realise that carb loading isn’t about eating ‘more’ food, but instead it's eating normal amounts of food with a higher relative carbohydrate content.

So, we reduce fat to make room for carbs. Limiting fibre in the last couple of days before the race also helped put my mind at ease regarding the chances of experiencing gastric distress on race day. It was a lesson learned the hard way...

I remember the night before a Coast to Coast race many years ago. I went to a local pub for dinner and ordered lamb shanks with a side of carrots and broccoli. I enjoyed a hearty feast of epic meat proportions and went to bed with a satisfyingly full tummy.

Unfortunately, during the mountain run stage the next day, I had stomach pains, bloating, and an inability to digest as much fuel as normal. It didn’t take long for my coach and I to blame the fatty and fibrous nature of my pre-race dinner for the tummy issues that ensued.

### The mental challenges

Carb loading comes at a time when energy expenditure through exercise is becoming less and less as training tapers off into race day. This helps support the saturation of glycogen in the body as less is being used, but it can also lead to some interesting mind games.

If someone wants to gain weight, they’ll generally achieve it if they exercise less but keep the same amount of food going in. I found it was very common (well, guaranteed actually) during the taper and carb loading phase to see the scales start to tip upwards by a kilogram or two.

Given bodyweight affects performance in sports that reward power-to-weight ratio (such as running and cycling), I always found it tricky to mentally accept my increasing weight as race day looms.

I remember going to one IRONMAN® registration and submitting an official pre-race weigh-in that felt embarrassing to admit to. But what I came to understand and appreciate better was how important the ‘weight’ in my body was.

We’d never start a long road trip in a car with an empty tank of gas, nor should we expect to draw much from ourselves physically on race day if we haven’t topped up our energy. Those extra kilograms showing on the scales before race day captured the extra fuel I had in the tank which would serve me well once the starter gun went off.

### Pre-race fueling

The ‘icing on the cake’ when it came to my pre-race carb loading was the energy gel I’d consume about 15 minutes prior to the start. Generally, by this stage, I would be finishing my warm-up, which likely would’ve taxed a little bit of my glycogen stores. I found it a psychological boost to take an extra 30-gram carbohydrate hit and know my stored energy was back at its maximum as we rolled into 'go-time'.

Fifteen minutes prior seemed long enough for me to feel it would digest okay as I sent my body into battle. Of course, the next challenge was meeting my carbohydrate and hydration demands for the entirety of the race duration. But if I nailed my carb loading in the days leading up, at least I knew I was getting off to the best possible start.

### Further reading

**Source:** https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/
**Title:** Creatine in Health and Disease

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/)Abstract

Although creatine has been mostly studied as an ergogenic aid for exercise, training, and sport, several health and potential therapeutic benefits have been reported. This is because creatine plays a critical role in cellular metabolism, particularly during metabolically stressed states, and limitations in the ability to transport and/or store creatine can impair metabolism. Moreover, increasing availability of creatine in tissue may enhance cellular metabolism and thereby lessen the severity of injury and/or disease conditions, particularly when oxygen availability is compromised. This systematic review assesses the peer-reviewed scientific and medical evidence related to creatine’s role in promoting general health as we age and how creatine supplementation has been used as a nutritional strategy to help individuals recover from injury and/or manage chronic disease. Additionally, it provides reasonable conclusions about the role of creatine on health and disease based on current scientific evidence. Based on this analysis, it can be concluded that creatine supplementation has several health and therapeutic benefits throughout the lifespan.

**Keywords:**ergogenic aids, cellular metabolism, phosphagens, sarcopenia, cognition, diabetes, creatine synthesis deficiencies, concussion, traumatic brain injury, spinal cord injury, muscle atrophy, rehabilitation, pregnancy, immunity, anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, anticancer

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/)1. Introduction

Creatine supplementation is one of the most studied and effective ergogenic aids for athletes [[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B1-nutrients-13-00447)]. The multifaceted mechanisms by which creatine exerts its beneficial effect include increasing anaerobic energy capacity, decreasing protein breakdown, leading to increased muscle mass and physical performance [[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B1-nutrients-13-00447)]. While these well-recognized creatine effects benefit the athlete, creatine may also serve as a potential clinical and therapeutic supplementary treatment to conventional medical interventions [[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B2-nutrients-13-00447),[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B3-nutrients-13-00447),[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B4-nutrients-13-00447),[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B5-nutrients-13-00447),[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B6-nutrients-13-00447),[7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B7-nutrients-13-00447),[8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B8-nutrients-13-00447),[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B9-nutrients-13-00447),[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B10-nutrients-13-00447)]. In this regard, over recent years, researchers have been investigating the potential therapeutic role of creatine supplementation on health-related conditions such as diabetes [[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B11-nutrients-13-00447)], sarcopenia [[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B4-nutrients-13-00447),[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B6-nutrients-13-00447),[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B12-nutrients-13-00447),[13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B13-nutrients-13-00447)], osteoporosis [[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B2-nutrients-13-00447),[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B14-nutrients-13-00447)], cancer [[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B10-nutrients-13-00447),[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B15-nutrients-13-00447),[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B16-nutrients-13-00447),[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B17-nutrients-13-00447),[18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B18-nutrients-13-00447)], rehabilitation [[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B4-nutrients-13-00447),[19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B19-nutrients-13-00447),[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B20-nutrients-13-00447),[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B21-nutrients-13-00447),[22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B22-nutrients-13-00447),[23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B23-nutrients-13-00447),[24](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B24-nutrients-13-00447),[25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B25-nutrients-13-00447),[26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B26-nutrients-13-00447)], cognition [[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B3-nutrients-13-00447),[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B27-nutrients-13-00447),[28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B28-nutrients-13-00447),[29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B29-nutrients-13-00447)], and cardiovascular health [[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B5-nutrients-13-00447),[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B6-nutrients-13-00447),[8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B8-nutrients-13-00447),[30](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B30-nutrients-13-00447),[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B31-nutrients-13-00447),[32](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B32-nutrients-13-00447)], among others. This work has increased interest in creatine use as a nutritional strategy to help maintain functional and mental capacity and, as we age, reduce risk to chronic disease, and/or serve as an adjunctive intervention to help manage disease and/or promote recovery. This special issue aims to provide comprehensive reviews of the role of creatine in health and clinical disease. To do so, we have invited a number of top creatine scholars to contribute comprehensive reviews as well as encouraged colleagues to submit meta-analyses and original research to this special issue.

As an introduction about creatine’s potential role in health and disease, the following provides a general overview of creatine’s metabolic role, purported benefits throughout the lifespan, and potential therapeutic applications. Additionally, we provide reasonable conclusions about the state of the science on creatine supplementation. This overview will be accompanied by separate, more comprehensive, literature reviews on the metabolic basis of creatine in health and disease as well as the potential role of creatine in pregnancy; children and adolescents; exercise and performance; physical therapy and rehabilitation; women’s health; aging, sarcopenia, and osteoporosis; brain neuroprotection and function; immunity, cancer protection and management; heart and muscle health; and, chronic and post-viral fatigue. We hope that this review and special issue will help readers and medical practitioners better understand the safety and efficacy of creatine supplementation in a variety of populations and provide recommendations about future research needs.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/)2. Methods

A systematic review of the scientific and medical literature was conducted to assess the state of the science related to creatine supplementation on metabolism, performance, health, and disease management. This was accomplished by doing keyword searches related to creatine supplementation on each topic summarized using the National Institutes for Health National Library of Medicine [PubMed.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/PubMed.gov) search engine. A total of 1322 articles were reviewed with relevant research highlighted in this systematic review.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/)3. Metabolic Role

Creatine (_N_-aminoiminomethyl-_N_-methyl glycine) is a naturally occurring and nitrogen-containing compound comprised from amino acids that is classified within the family of guanidine phosphagens [[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B1-nutrients-13-00447),[33](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B33-nutrients-13-00447)]. Creatine is synthesized endogenously from arginine and glycine by arginine glycine amidinotransferase (AGAT) to guanidinoacetate (GAA). The GAA is then methylated by the enzyme guanidinoacetate N-methyltransferase (GAMT) with S-adenosyl methionine (SAMe) to form creatine [[34](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B34-nutrients-13-00447)]. The kidney, pancreas, liver, and some regions in the brain contain AGAT with most GAA formed in the kidney and converted by GMAT to creatine in the liver [[35](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B35-nutrients-13-00447),[36](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B36-nutrients-13-00447),[37](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B37-nutrients-13-00447)]. Endogenous creatine synthesis provides about half of the daily need for creatine [[35](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B35-nutrients-13-00447)]. The remaining amount of creatine needed to maintain normal tissue levels of creatine is obtained in the diet primarily from red meat and fish [[38](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B38-nutrients-13-00447),[39](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B39-nutrients-13-00447),[40](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B40-nutrients-13-00447),[41](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B41-nutrients-13-00447)] or dietary supplements [[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B1-nutrients-13-00447),[42](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B42-nutrients-13-00447),[43](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B43-nutrients-13-00447)]. About 95% of creatine is stored in muscle with the remaining amount found in other tissues, like the heart, brain, and testes [[44](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B44-nutrients-13-00447),[45](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B45-nutrients-13-00447)]. Of this, about 2/3 of creatine is bound with inorganic phosphate (Pi) and stored as phosphocreatine (PCr) with the remainder stored as free creatine (Cr). The total creatine pool (Cr + PCr) is about 120 mmol/kg of dry muscle mass for a 70 kg individual who maintains a diet that includes red meat and fish. Vegetarians have been reported to have muscle creatine and PCr stores about 20–30% lower than non-vegetarians [[46](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B46-nutrients-13-00447),[47](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B47-nutrients-13-00447)]. The body breaks down about 1–2% of creatine in the muscle per day into creatinine which is excreted in the urine [[46](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B46-nutrients-13-00447),[48](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B48-nutrients-13-00447),[49](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B49-nutrients-13-00447)]. Degradation of creatine to creatinine is greater in individuals with larger muscle mass and individuals with higher physical activity levels. Therefore, a normal-sized individual may need to consume 2–3 g/day of creatine to maintain normal creatine stores depending on diet, muscle mass, and physical activity levels. In fact, Wallimann and colleagues [[50](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B50-nutrients-13-00447)] noted that since creatine stores are not fully saturated on vegan or normal omnivore diets that generally provide 0 or 0.75–1.5 g/day of creatine, daily dietary creatine needs may be in the order of 2–4 g/person/day to promote general health [[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B1-nutrients-13-00447),[50](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B50-nutrients-13-00447)]. The most effective and rapid way to increase muscle creatine stores is to ingest 5 g of creatine monohydrate four times daily for 5–7 days (i.e., 0.3 g/kg/day) [[46](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B46-nutrients-13-00447),[49](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B49-nutrients-13-00447)]. However, some studies have shown that consuming 2–3 g/day of creatine for 30 days can also effectively increase muscle creatine stores [[46](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B46-nutrients-13-00447),[49](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B49-nutrients-13-00447)]. Dietary supplementation of 20–30 g/day of creatine monohydrate for up to 5 years has also been studied in some clinical populations who need higher levels to increase brain concentrations of creatine, offset creatine synthesis deficiencies, or influence disease states [[51](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B51-nutrients-13-00447),[52](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B52-nutrients-13-00447),[53](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B53-nutrients-13-00447)].

Creatine and phosphagens play a critical role in providing energy through the creatine kinase (CK) and PCr system [[50](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B50-nutrients-13-00447),[54](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B54-nutrients-13-00447),[55](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B55-nutrients-13-00447)]. In this regard, the free energy yielded from the enzymatic degradation of adenosine triphosphate (ATP) into adenosine diphosphate (ADP) and Pi by CK serves as a primary fuel to replenish ATP for cellular metabolism. Breaking down PCr into Pi and Cr with the enzyme CK yields about 10.3 kcals of free energy that can be used to resynthesize ADP -+ Pi into ATP [[38](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B38-nutrients-13-00447),[39](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B39-nutrients-13-00447),[56](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B56-nutrients-13-00447),[57](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B57-nutrients-13-00447)]. The ability to replenish depleted ATP levels during high-energy demand states like intense exercise or in conditions where energy production is either impaired (e.g., ischemia, hypoxia) or insufficient due to increased demand (e.g., mental fatigue, some disease states) is important in maintaining ATP availability.

Creatine enters the cytosol through creatine transporters (CRTR) [[58](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B58-nutrients-13-00447),[59](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B59-nutrients-13-00447),[60](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B60-nutrients-13-00447),[61](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B61-nutrients-13-00447)]. In the cytosol, creatine and associated cytosolic and glycolytic CK isoforms help maintain glycolytic ATP levels, the cytosolic ATP/ADP ratio, and cytosolic ATP-consumption [[50](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B50-nutrients-13-00447)]. Additionally, creatine diffuses into the mitochondria and couples with ATP produced from oxidative phosphorylation and the adenine nucleotide translocator (ANT) via mitochondrial CK. PCr then diffuse back into the cytosol and help meet energy needs. This coupling reduces the formation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and therefore creatine acts as a direct and/or indirect antioxidant [[18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B18-nutrients-13-00447),[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B21-nutrients-13-00447),[62](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B62-nutrients-13-00447),[63](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B63-nutrients-13-00447)]. The creatine phosphate shuttle is important in translocating ATP produced from oxidative phosphorylation in the mitochondrial to the cytosol and areas within the cell needing ATP for energy metabolism [[50](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B50-nutrients-13-00447),[56](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B56-nutrients-13-00447),[57](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B57-nutrients-13-00447)]. The creatine phosphate shuttle thereby serves as an important regulator of cellular metabolism. The role of creatine in energy metabolism and impact that creatine has on maintaining energy availability in diseases that depend on the CK/PCr system provides the metabolic basis on how creatine can affect health, disease, and provide therapeutic benefit [[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B6-nutrients-13-00447),[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B9-nutrients-13-00447),[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B21-nutrients-13-00447),[41](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B41-nutrients-13-00447),[50](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B50-nutrients-13-00447),[64](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B64-nutrients-13-00447),[65](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B65-nutrients-13-00447),[66](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B66-nutrients-13-00447),[67](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B67-nutrients-13-00447),[68](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B68-nutrients-13-00447),[69](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B69-nutrients-13-00447),[70](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B70-nutrients-13-00447),[71](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B71-nutrients-13-00447)]. The role of creatine in energy metabolism will be discussed in greater detail in another paper in this special issue.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/)4. General Health Benefits

Most creatine research initially focused on creatine’s role in exercise performance, training adaptations, and safety in untrained and trained healthy individuals [[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B1-nutrients-13-00447)]. Creatine supplementation has been reported to increase muscle creatine and PCr levels, enhance acute exercise capacity, and improve training adaptations [[44](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B44-nutrients-13-00447),[66](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B66-nutrients-13-00447),[69](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B69-nutrients-13-00447),[72](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B72-nutrients-13-00447),[73](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B73-nutrients-13-00447),[74](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B74-nutrients-13-00447),[75](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B75-nutrients-13-00447),[76](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B76-nutrients-13-00447),[77](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B77-nutrients-13-00447),[78](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B78-nutrients-13-00447),[79](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B79-nutrients-13-00447),[80](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B80-nutrients-13-00447),[81](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B81-nutrients-13-00447),[82](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B82-nutrients-13-00447),[83](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B83-nutrients-13-00447),[84](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B84-nutrients-13-00447),[85](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B85-nutrients-13-00447),[86](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B86-nutrients-13-00447),[87](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B87-nutrients-13-00447),[88](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B88-nutrients-13-00447),[89](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B89-nutrients-13-00447),[90](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B90-nutrients-13-00447),[91](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B91-nutrients-13-00447),[92](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B92-nutrients-13-00447),[93](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B93-nutrients-13-00447),[94](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B94-nutrients-13-00447),[95](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B95-nutrients-13-00447),[96](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B96-nutrients-13-00447)]. The improvement in performance has generally been 10–20% on various high-intensity exercise tasks [[97](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B97-nutrients-13-00447)] that include lifetime fitness activities like fitness/weight training [[77](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B77-nutrients-13-00447),[84](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B84-nutrients-13-00447),[91](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B91-nutrients-13-00447),[98](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B98-nutrients-13-00447),[99](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B99-nutrients-13-00447),[100](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B100-nutrients-13-00447),[101](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B101-nutrients-13-00447),[102](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B102-nutrients-13-00447),[103](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B103-nutrients-13-00447),[104](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B104-nutrients-13-00447),[105](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B105-nutrients-13-00447),[106](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B106-nutrients-13-00447),[107](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B107-nutrients-13-00447),[108](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B108-nutrients-13-00447)], golf [[109](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B109-nutrients-13-00447)], volleyball [[110](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B110-nutrients-13-00447)], soccer [[82](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B82-nutrients-13-00447),[111](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B111-nutrients-13-00447),[112](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B112-nutrients-13-00447)], softball [[113](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B113-nutrients-13-00447)], ice hockey [[114](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B114-nutrients-13-00447)], running [[115](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B115-nutrients-13-00447),[116](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B116-nutrients-13-00447),[117](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B117-nutrients-13-00447),[118](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B118-nutrients-13-00447),[119](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B119-nutrients-13-00447)], and swimming [[73](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B73-nutrients-13-00447),[74](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B74-nutrients-13-00447),[120](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B120-nutrients-13-00447),[121](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B121-nutrients-13-00447),[122](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B122-nutrients-13-00447),[123](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B123-nutrients-13-00447)], among others. Ergogenic benefits have been reported in men and women from children to elderly populations, although the majority of studies have been conducted on men [[74](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B74-nutrients-13-00447),[111](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B111-nutrients-13-00447),[113](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B113-nutrients-13-00447),[124](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B124-nutrients-13-00447),[125](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B125-nutrients-13-00447),[126](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B126-nutrients-13-00447),[127](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B127-nutrients-13-00447),[128](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B128-nutrients-13-00447)]. After comprehensively reviewing the literature, the International Society of Sports Nutrition (ISSN) concluded that creatine is “the most effective ergogenic nutritional supplement currently available to athletes in terms of increasing high-intensity exercise capacity and lean body mass during training” [[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B1-nutrients-13-00447),[42](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B42-nutrients-13-00447),[44](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B44-nutrients-13-00447),[89](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B89-nutrients-13-00447)]. The American Dietetic Association, Dietitians of Canada, and the American College of Sports Medicine have come to similar conclusions in their position stands [[129](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B129-nutrients-13-00447),[130](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B130-nutrients-13-00447)]. Thus, there is a strong scientific consensus that creatine supplementation is an effective ergogenic nutrient for athletes as well as individuals starting a health and fitness program.

As performance-related studies assessed health and safety markers, evidence began to accumulate that creatine supplementation may also offer some health and/or therapeutic benefits as we age [[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B4-nutrients-13-00447),[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B12-nutrients-13-00447),[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B14-nutrients-13-00447),[67](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B67-nutrients-13-00447),[69](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B69-nutrients-13-00447),[70](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B70-nutrients-13-00447),[71](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B71-nutrients-13-00447),[131](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B131-nutrients-13-00447)]. In this regard, creatine supplementation has been reported to help lower cholesterol, triglycerides and/or manage blood lipid levels [[77](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B77-nutrients-13-00447),[132](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B132-nutrients-13-00447),[133](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B133-nutrients-13-00447)]; reduce the accumulation of fat on the liver [[133](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B133-nutrients-13-00447),[134](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B134-nutrients-13-00447)]; decrease homocysteine thereby reducing risk of heart disease [[30](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B30-nutrients-13-00447),[135](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B135-nutrients-13-00447)]; serve as an antioxidant [[30](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B30-nutrients-13-00447),[136](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B136-nutrients-13-00447),[137](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B137-nutrients-13-00447),[138](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B138-nutrients-13-00447),[139](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B139-nutrients-13-00447)]; enhance glycemic control [[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B1-nutrients-13-00447),[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B11-nutrients-13-00447),[140](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B140-nutrients-13-00447),[141](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B141-nutrients-13-00447),[142](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B142-nutrients-13-00447),[143](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B143-nutrients-13-00447)]; reduce the progress of some forms of cancer [[8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B8-nutrients-13-00447),[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B17-nutrients-13-00447),[18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B18-nutrients-13-00447),[135](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B135-nutrients-13-00447),[144](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B144-nutrients-13-00447),[145](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B145-nutrients-13-00447),[146](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B146-nutrients-13-00447),[147](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B147-nutrients-13-00447)]; increase strength and muscle mass [[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B2-nutrients-13-00447),[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B9-nutrients-13-00447),[13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B13-nutrients-13-00447),[67](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B67-nutrients-13-00447),[70](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B70-nutrients-13-00447),[71](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B71-nutrients-13-00447),[93](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B93-nutrients-13-00447),[99](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B99-nutrients-13-00447),[101](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B101-nutrients-13-00447),[148](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B148-nutrients-13-00447),[149](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B149-nutrients-13-00447),[150](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B150-nutrients-13-00447),[151](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B151-nutrients-13-00447),[152](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B152-nutrients-13-00447),[153](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B153-nutrients-13-00447),[154](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B154-nutrients-13-00447)]; minimize bone loss in some studies [[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B2-nutrients-13-00447),[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B4-nutrients-13-00447),[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B14-nutrients-13-00447),[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B16-nutrients-13-00447),[99](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B99-nutrients-13-00447),[150](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B150-nutrients-13-00447),[155](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B155-nutrients-13-00447),[156](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B156-nutrients-13-00447),[157](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B157-nutrients-13-00447),[158](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B158-nutrients-13-00447),[159](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B159-nutrients-13-00447),[160](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B160-nutrients-13-00447)]; improve functional capacity in osteoarthritic and fibromyalgia patients [[22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B22-nutrients-13-00447),[161](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B161-nutrients-13-00447),[162](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B162-nutrients-13-00447)]; enhance cognitive function particularly in older populations [[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B3-nutrients-13-00447),[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B27-nutrients-13-00447),[28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B28-nutrients-13-00447),[69](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B69-nutrients-13-00447),[94](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B94-nutrients-13-00447),[127](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B127-nutrients-13-00447),[131](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B131-nutrients-13-00447),[159](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B159-nutrients-13-00447),[163](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B163-nutrients-13-00447),[164](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B164-nutrients-13-00447),[165](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B165-nutrients-13-00447),[166](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B166-nutrients-13-00447),[167](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B167-nutrients-13-00447),[168](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B168-nutrients-13-00447)]; and, in some instances, improve the efficacy of some anti-depressant medications [[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B5-nutrients-13-00447),[29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B29-nutrients-13-00447),[169](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B169-nutrients-13-00447),[170](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B170-nutrients-13-00447),[171](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B171-nutrients-13-00447),[172](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B172-nutrients-13-00447)]. These findings support contentions that it is prudent for individuals to consume at least 3 g/day of creatine to support general health as one ages [[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B1-nutrients-13-00447),[50](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B50-nutrients-13-00447)]. Therefore, although more research is needed, it can be reasonably concluded based on current evidence that creatine supplementation can increase cellular energy availability and support general health, fitness, and well-being throughout the lifespan.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/)5. Role of Creatine in Aging Populations

Several studies have evaluated the effects of creatine supplementation in older populations in an attempt to prevent sarcopenia, maintain strength, and/or reduce the risk of chronic disease. The following discusses some of these potential applications.

### 5.1. Muscle Mass, Strength, Bone and Body Composition

Sarcopenia is an age-related muscle condition characterized by a reduction in muscle quantity, muscle strength, and functional capacity. Although multifactorial, sarcopenia may be caused by changes in muscle protein kinetics (synthesis and breakdown), neuromuscular function, inflammation, physical activity, and nutrition [[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B12-nutrients-13-00447),[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B14-nutrients-13-00447)]. We also generally lose strength, muscle mass, bone mass, balance while increasing body fat as we age, whether clinically diagnosed with sarcopenia or not [[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B3-nutrients-13-00447),[69](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B69-nutrients-13-00447),[131](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B131-nutrients-13-00447)]. A number of nutritional and exercise interventions have been suggested to counteract sarcopenia in older individuals, including creatine supplementation during resistance training [[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B12-nutrients-13-00447),[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B14-nutrients-13-00447)]. For example, Brose and colleagues [[173](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B173-nutrients-13-00447)] were among the first to report that creatine supplementation (5 g/day for 14 weeks) during heavy resistance training promoted greater gains in muscle mass and isometric muscle strength in older adults (>65 years). Chrusch and coworkers [[106](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B106-nutrients-13-00447)] reported that older participants (60–84 years) who supplemented their diet with creatine (0.3 g/kg/day for 5 days and 0.07 g/kg/day for 79 days) during supervised resistance training (3 days/week for 12 weeks) experienced greater gains in lean tissue mass, lower-body maximal strength, and endurance, and isokinetic knee flexion/extension power compared to controls. Candow and colleagues [[99](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B99-nutrients-13-00447)] reported that creatine (0.1 g/kg/day) and protein (0.3 g/kg/day) supplementation increased muscle mass and strength while decreasing protein degradation and bone resorption markers in older men. Chilibeck and associates [[150](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B150-nutrients-13-00447)] found that creatine supplementation (0.1 g/kg/day) during 12 months of resistance training increased strength and bone density in postmenopausal women. Gualano and coworkers [[98](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B98-nutrients-13-00447)] reported that creatine supplementation (20 g/day for 5 days; 5 g/day for 161 days) during resistance training improved appendicular lean mass and muscle function in older vulnerable women and that creatine supplementation alone resulted in similar gains in muscle mass compared to those engaged in resistance training alone. Aguiar and coworkers [[96](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B96-nutrients-13-00447)] also found that creatine supplementation (5 g/day for 12 weeks) combined with resistance training improved muscle endurance, ability to perform functional tasks, maximal strength, and muscle mass in older women.

Additionally, McMorris et al. [[174](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B174-nutrients-13-00447)] reported that creatine supplementation (20 g/day for 7 days) after sleep deprivation improved balance measures. Bernat and colleagues [[175](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B175-nutrients-13-00447)] reported that creatine supplementation (0.1 g/kg/day) during 8 weeks of high-velocity resistance training in untrained healthy aging men promoted significantly greater gains in leg press and total lower-body strength, muscle thickness, and some measures of peak torque and physical performance. Moreover, a meta-analysis revealed that older individuals participating in resistance training experienced greater gains in muscle mass, strength, and functional capacity when supplementing their diet with creatine [[91](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B91-nutrients-13-00447)]. A similar meta-analysis conducted by Candow and colleagues [[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B9-nutrients-13-00447)] found that older individuals who took creatine during resistance training experienced significantly greater gains in muscle mass and upper body. While not all studies report statistically significant effects, the preponderance of available research supports contentions that creatine supplementation, when combined with resistance exercise, can help maintain or increase muscle mass, strength, and balance in older individuals and therefore serve as an effective countermeasure to attenuate sarcopenia. The role of creatine supplementation during resistance training in sarcopenic populations will be discussed in more detail in this paper series on aging, sarcopenia, and bone health.

In addition, people often experience adult-onset obesity as they age, prompting them to diet to promote weight loss. Unfortunately, this often leads to loss of muscle mass and strength, which would be counterproductive in older individuals. Creatine supplementation while following an energy-restricted diet may be an effective strategy to maintain muscle mass, promote fat loss, and help manage adult-onset obesity. In support of this contention, Forbes and colleagues [[176](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B176-nutrients-13-00447)] recently conducted a meta-analysis on the effects of creatine on body composition and found that creatine supplementation may not only help maintain muscle mass but also promote fat mass loss. This strategy could be helpful in preventing or managing adult-onset obesity. Thus, although more research is needed, it can be reasonably concluded based on available literature that creatine supplementation, particularly when combined with resistance training, can promote gains in strength and help maintain or increase muscle mass and bone density in older individuals. Further, creatine supplementation during energy-restriction-induced weight loss interventions may be an effective way to preserve muscle mass, promote fat loss, and thereby help manage adult-onset obesity.

### 5.2. Cognitive Function

Creatine supplementation has been reported to increase brain PCr content by 5–15% and thereby enhance brain bioenergetics [[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B21-nutrients-13-00447),[53](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B53-nutrients-13-00447),[69](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B69-nutrients-13-00447),[131](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B131-nutrients-13-00447),[171](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B171-nutrients-13-00447)]. Consequently, research has examined whether creatine supplementation affects cognition, memory, and/or executive function in older individuals as well as patients with mild cognitive impairment [[94](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B94-nutrients-13-00447),[168](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B168-nutrients-13-00447),[174](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B174-nutrients-13-00447),[177](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B177-nutrients-13-00447),[178](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B178-nutrients-13-00447)]. Several studies have found that creatine supplementation attenuates mental fatigue [[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B27-nutrients-13-00447),[28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B28-nutrients-13-00447),[127](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B127-nutrients-13-00447)] and/or can improve cognition, executive function, and/or memory [[28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B28-nutrients-13-00447),[94](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B94-nutrients-13-00447),[127](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B127-nutrients-13-00447),[168](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B168-nutrients-13-00447),[177](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B177-nutrients-13-00447),[179](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B179-nutrients-13-00447)]. For example, Watanabe and associates [[180](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B180-nutrients-13-00447)] found that creatine supplementation (8 g/day for 5 days) increased oxygen utilization in the brain and reduced mental fatigue in participants performing repetitive mathematical calculations. Rae et al. [[177](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B177-nutrients-13-00447)] found that working memory and processing speed increased with creatine supplementation (5 g/day for 6 weeks). McMorris and colleagues [[174](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B174-nutrients-13-00447)] reported that sleep-deprived participants better maintained random movement generation, time to react to choices, mood state, and balance when supplemented with creatine (20 g/day for 7 days). These researchers also reported that random number generation, forward spatial recall, and long-term memory tasks were significantly improved in elderly participants when supplemented with creatine. Ling et al. [[178](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B178-nutrients-13-00447)] also reported that cognition on some tasks was improved with creatine ethyl ester supplementation (5 g/day for 15 days). More recently, VAN Cutsem and coworkers [[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B27-nutrients-13-00447)] reported that creatine supplementation (20 g/day for 7 days) prior to performing a simulated soccer match improved muscular endurance and prolonged cognitive performance. While more research is needed and not all studies show benefit [[127](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B127-nutrients-13-00447),[167](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B167-nutrients-13-00447)], it can be reasonably concluded based on current scientific evidence that creatine supplementation may increase brain creatine content and/or support cognitive function, particularly as one ages.

### 5.3. Glucose Management and Diabetes

Creatine uptake into tissue is influenced by glucose and insulin [[142](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B142-nutrients-13-00447),[181](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B181-nutrients-13-00447),[182](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B182-nutrients-13-00447)]. Creatine supplementation has also been reported to prevent declines in the GLUT-4 transporter during immobilization while increasing GLUT-4 by 40% during rehabilitation after atrophy [[140](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B140-nutrients-13-00447)]. Moreover, co-ingestion of creatine with carbohydrate [[47](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B47-nutrients-13-00447),[183](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B183-nutrients-13-00447)] or creatine with carbohydrate and protein [[184](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B184-nutrients-13-00447)] has been reported to increase creatine uptake and/or muscle glycogen levels [[47](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B47-nutrients-13-00447),[184](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B184-nutrients-13-00447),[185](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B185-nutrients-13-00447)]. Consequently, research has evaluated whether creatine supplementation may influence glucose management [[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B10-nutrients-13-00447),[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B11-nutrients-13-00447),[140](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B140-nutrients-13-00447),[141](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B141-nutrients-13-00447),[142](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B142-nutrients-13-00447),[143](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B143-nutrients-13-00447)]. For example, Gualano et al. [[141](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B141-nutrients-13-00447)] evaluated the effects of creatine supplementation (5 g/day for 12 weeks) during training in participants with type 2 diabetes. The researchers found that creatine supplementation improved glucose tolerance to ingesting a standard meal, increased GLUT-4 translocation, and promoted a significant reduction in HbA1c levels. Moreover, the AMPK-alpha protein content tended to be higher after Cr supplementation and was significantly related to the changes in GLUT-4 translocation and Hb1Ac levels, suggesting that AMPK signaling may be implicated in the effects of supplementation on glucose uptake in type 2 diabetes [[143](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B143-nutrients-13-00447)]. Thus, there is evidence to suggest that creatine supplementation enhances glucose uptake and insulin sensitivity and, therefore, can help individuals manage glucose and HbA1c levels, particularly when initiating an exercise program [[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B10-nutrients-13-00447),[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B11-nutrients-13-00447),[186](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B186-nutrients-13-00447)]. Based on this literature, it can be reasonably concluded that **c**reatine supplementation may support healthy glucose management.

### 5.4. Heart Disease

Coronary artery disease limits blood supply to the heart, thereby increasing susceptibility to ischemic events, arrhythmias, and/or heart failure. Creatine and PCr play an important role in maintaining myocardial bioenergetics during ischemic events [[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B21-nutrients-13-00447)]. For this reason, there has been interest in assessing the role of creatine or PCr administration in reducing arrhythmias, ischemia-related damage, and/or heart function in individuals with chronic heart failure [[187](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B187-nutrients-13-00447),[188](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B188-nutrients-13-00447),[189](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B189-nutrients-13-00447),[190](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B190-nutrients-13-00447),[191](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B191-nutrients-13-00447),[192](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B192-nutrients-13-00447),[193](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B193-nutrients-13-00447),[194](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B194-nutrients-13-00447),[195](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B195-nutrients-13-00447),[196](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B196-nutrients-13-00447),[197](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B197-nutrients-13-00447)]. For example, Anyukhovsky et al. [[195](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B195-nutrients-13-00447)] reported that intravenous administration of PCr and phosphocreatinine (300 mg/kg) in canines prevented the accumulation of lysophosphoglycerides in the ischemic zone of the heart, which is associated with an increased prevalence of arrhythmias. The researchers concluded that this might explain the antiarrhythmic action of PCr and phosphocreatinine in acute myocardial ischemia. Sharov and coworkers [[194](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B194-nutrients-13-00447)] reported that exogenous PCr administration protected against ischemia in the heart. Likewise, Balestrino and coworkers [[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B21-nutrients-13-00447)] evaluated the effects of adding PCr to cardioplegic solutions on energy availability during myocardial ischemia. The researchers found that PCr administration improved energy availability to the heart, reduced the incidence of arrhythmias, and improved myocardial function. As noted below, there is also evidence that creatine supplementation may maintain energy availability during brain ischemia and reduce stroke-related damage. Moreover, several studies have reported some benefit of oral creatine supplementation in heart failure patients participating in rehabilitation programs [[198](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B198-nutrients-13-00447),[199](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B199-nutrients-13-00447),[200](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B200-nutrients-13-00447),[201](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B201-nutrients-13-00447)]. While not all studies report benefit from oral creatine supplementation [[23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B23-nutrients-13-00447),[202](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B202-nutrients-13-00447)] and more research is needed, current evidence suggests that phospho**c**reatine administration and possibly creatine supplementation support heart metabolism and health, particularly during ischemic challenges.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/)6. Potential Therapeutic Role of Creatine Supplementation

Given the metabolic role of creatine and the PCR/CK system, particularly during ischemia and in some disease states, there has been interest in examining the potential therapeutic role of creatine in a number of clinical populations. The following provides a brief overview of some of this work as an introduction to topics that will be reviewed in greater detail in other papers in this special issue.

### 6.1. Creatine Synthesis Deficiencies

Some individuals are born with rare deficiencies in creatine-related enzymes or transporters (e.g., AGAT, GAMT, and CRTR) that reduce the ability to transport creatine into the cell or synthesize creatine endogenously [[203](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B203-nutrients-13-00447)]. There is also recent evidence that the human genome encodes 19 genes of the solute carrier 6 (SLC6) family and that non-synonymous changes in the coding sequence give rise to mutated or misfolded transporters that cause diseases in affected individuals [[204](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B204-nutrients-13-00447)]. This includes the creatine transporter (CT1, SLC6A8) in which deficiencies have been reported to account for about 2% of intellectual disabilities in boys [[205](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B205-nutrients-13-00447)]. Individuals with creatine synthesis deficiencies and creatine transporter mutations typically present with low brain Cr and PCr levels [[53](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B53-nutrients-13-00447),[61](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B61-nutrients-13-00447),[204](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B204-nutrients-13-00447),[206](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B206-nutrients-13-00447),[207](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B207-nutrients-13-00447),[208](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B208-nutrients-13-00447),[209](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B209-nutrients-13-00447),[210](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B210-nutrients-13-00447)]. Low brain creatine content has been associated with muscle myopathies (e.g., weakness), voluntary or involuntary movement disorders that can affect muscle function and coordination, speech development, epilepsy, cognitive and motor development delays, and/or autism [[53](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B53-nutrients-13-00447),[61](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B61-nutrients-13-00447),[203](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B203-nutrients-13-00447),[204](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B204-nutrients-13-00447),[206](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B206-nutrients-13-00447),[207](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B207-nutrients-13-00447),[208](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B208-nutrients-13-00447),[209](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B209-nutrients-13-00447),[210](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B210-nutrients-13-00447)]. Individuals with these conditions have a greater dependence on dietary creatine. For this reason, high-dose, long-term creatine supplementation (e.g., 0.3–0.8 g/kg/day) throughout the lifespan is a nutritional strategy of increasing brain creatine content in these populations [[53](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B53-nutrients-13-00447),[61](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B61-nutrients-13-00447),[203](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B203-nutrients-13-00447),[204](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B204-nutrients-13-00447),[206](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B206-nutrients-13-00447),[207](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B207-nutrients-13-00447),[208](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B208-nutrients-13-00447),[209](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B209-nutrients-13-00447),[210](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B210-nutrients-13-00447),[211](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B211-nutrients-13-00447),[212](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B212-nutrients-13-00447),[213](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B213-nutrients-13-00447),[214](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B214-nutrients-13-00447)]. This research has generally found that long-term creatine supplementation can improve clinical outcomes, particularly in patients with AGAT and GAMT deficiencies [[207](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B207-nutrients-13-00447)].

For example, Bianchi et al. [[215](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B215-nutrients-13-00447)] found that creatine supplementation (200–800 mg/kg/day divided into 5 servings per day) significantly increased brain creatine and PCr levels in patients with GAMT-d and AGAT-d creatine synthesis deficiencies. Battini et al. [[216](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B216-nutrients-13-00447)] reported that a patient diagnosed at birth with AGAT deficiency who was treated with creatine supplementation beginning at four months of age experienced normal psychomotor development at eighteen months compared to siblings who did not have the deficiency. Stockler-Ipsiroglu and coworkers [[217](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B217-nutrients-13-00447)] evaluated the effects of creatine monohydrate supplementation (0.3–0.8 g/kg/day) in 48 children with GMAT deficiency with clinical manifestations of global developmental delay/intellectual disability (DD/ID) with speech/language delay and behavioral problems (_n_ = 44), epilepsy (_n_ = 35), or movement disorder (_n_ = 13). The median age at treatment was 25.5 months, 39 months, and 11 years in patients with mild, moderate, and severe DD/ID, respectively. The researchers found that creatine supplementation increased brain creatine levels and improved or stabilized clinical symptoms. Moreover, four patients treated younger than nine months had normal or almost normal developmental outcomes. Long-term creatine supplementation has also been used to treat patients with ornithine aminotransferase (OAT) deficiency that causes gyrate atrophy of the choroid and retina due to secondary creatine depletion that is characterized by progressive vision loss [[218](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B218-nutrients-13-00447),[219](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B219-nutrients-13-00447),[220](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B220-nutrients-13-00447),[221](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B221-nutrients-13-00447),[222](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B222-nutrients-13-00447)]. These findings and others provide promise that high-dose creatine monohydrate supplementation is well tolerated and may be an effective adjunctive therapy for infants, children, and adults, particularly with AGAT deficiency [[207](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B207-nutrients-13-00447),[223](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B223-nutrients-13-00447),[224](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B224-nutrients-13-00447),[225](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B225-nutrients-13-00447),[226](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B226-nutrients-13-00447)]. Thus, it can be reasonably concluded that long-term, high-dose creatine supplementation in individuals with creatine synthesis can increase brain creatine and PCr levels and reduce the severity of deficits associated with these disorders.

### 6.2. Neurodegenerative Diseases and Muscular Dystrophy

Several studies have investigated the short- and long-term therapeutic benefit of creatine supplementation in animals, children, and adults with various neuromuscular diseases like Huntington’s disease (HD) [[51](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B51-nutrients-13-00447),[227](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B227-nutrients-13-00447),[228](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B228-nutrients-13-00447),[229](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B229-nutrients-13-00447),[230](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B230-nutrients-13-00447),[231](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B231-nutrients-13-00447),[232](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B232-nutrients-13-00447)]; Parkinson’s disease (PD) [[51](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B51-nutrients-13-00447),[66](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B66-nutrients-13-00447),[100](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B100-nutrients-13-00447),[227](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B227-nutrients-13-00447),[233](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B233-nutrients-13-00447),[234](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B234-nutrients-13-00447),[235](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B235-nutrients-13-00447)]; mitochondria-related diseases [[58](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B58-nutrients-13-00447),[235](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B235-nutrients-13-00447),[236](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B236-nutrients-13-00447),[237](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B237-nutrients-13-00447),[238](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B238-nutrients-13-00447),[239](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B239-nutrients-13-00447)]; amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) [[227](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B227-nutrients-13-00447),[240](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B240-nutrients-13-00447),[241](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B241-nutrients-13-00447),[242](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B242-nutrients-13-00447),[243](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B243-nutrients-13-00447),[244](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B244-nutrients-13-00447),[245](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B245-nutrients-13-00447),[246](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B246-nutrients-13-00447)]; spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy [[247](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B247-nutrients-13-00447)]; and, muscular dystrophies (MD) [[248](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B248-nutrients-13-00447),[249](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B249-nutrients-13-00447),[250](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B250-nutrients-13-00447),[251](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B251-nutrients-13-00447),[252](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B252-nutrients-13-00447),[253](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B253-nutrients-13-00447)]. Several of these investigations, particularly in animal models, reported improved exercise tolerance and/or clinical outcomes. However, a large multi-site clinical trial conducted by Bender and coworkers [[51](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B51-nutrients-13-00447)] on PD, HD, and ALS patients did not find promising results. In this regard, they monitored 1687 participants who supplemented their diet with creatine (9.5 g/day for up to 5 years). The researchers did not observe statistically significant improvement in PD or ALS patient outcomes. However, in patients with HD, there was some evidence that creatine supplementation attenuated brain atrophy, suggesting some potential clinical benefit in this population. The reason animal studies may have yielded more promising results may be due to the fact that people typically do not present with symptoms of neurodegenerative disorders (e.g., ALS, HD, PD, etc.) until they have lost 70% or more of their alpha neurons. On the other hand, results in muscular dystrophy populations have been more promising because the muscle is the primary target. To support this contention, Kley and coworkers [[254](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B254-nutrients-13-00447)] conducted a Cochrane systemic review of the literature and found that high-quality evidence from randomized clinical trials (RCTs) demonstrated that short- and medium-term creatine supplementation increases muscle strength in muscular dystrophies and functional performance in muscular dystrophy and idiopathic inflammatory myopathy. However, assessment of high quality RCTs found no significant improvement in muscle strength in metabolic myopathies [[254](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B254-nutrients-13-00447)]. Thus, while creatine supplementation has been shown to have neuroprotective properties and improve muscle strength and endurance in patient populations, the efficacy of long-term, high-dose creatine supplementation in individuals with neurodegenerative diseases is currently equivocal, while promising, in patients with muscular dystrophy.

### 6.3. Brain and Spinal Cord Neuroprotection

It is well known that creatine supplementation increases brain bioenergetics [[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B21-nutrients-13-00447),[166](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B166-nutrients-13-00447),[215](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B215-nutrients-13-00447),[235](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B235-nutrients-13-00447),[255](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B255-nutrients-13-00447),[256](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B256-nutrients-13-00447)] and has neuroprotective benefits, particularly in response to injury and/or ischemic conditions [[58](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B58-nutrients-13-00447),[64](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B64-nutrients-13-00447),[66](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B66-nutrients-13-00447),[257](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910963/#B257-nutrients-13-00447)]. Consequently, there has been interest in determining the effects of creatine supplementation on cerebral ischemia, stroke, traumatic brain injury (TBI), and spinal cord injury (SCI).
